episodes.212755: During the 16th late afternoon and evening, a warm, humid airmass interacting with an approaching cold front and associated upper wave triggered scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Moderate instability and vertical wind shear promoted organized multicells and some supercells.||There were several severe hail reports, with diameters ranging from 1.00 and 1.25 inches impacting Carroll, Tippecanoe, Putnam, Hendricks, Marion, and Hancock counties. Straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts estimated between 58 mph and 60 mph also downed trees and large tree limbs across portions of Parke, Vigo, Putnam, and Morgan counties.||The primary severe event was a tornadic thunderstorm that tracked from Putnam County into western Morgan County. An EF-1 tornado touched down in Putnam County around 7:45 PM EST, with estimated maximum wind speeds of 105 mph. The tornado damaged several residences, destroyed an outbuilding, heavily impacted a mobile home, and snapped many trees. The tornado tracked along an 8.24-mile path across Putnam County before crossing into western Morgan County at 8:01 PM EST, weakening to an EF-0 with estimated peak winds of 70 mph. The tornado tracked an additional 1.13 miles causing minor tree damage before dissipating. The total path length was 9.37 miles. This severe weather event would be the fourth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.
episodes.212882: Several clusters of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front across east-central Wisconsin during the afternoon on Tuesday (6/16).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to quarter size in the Fox Valley.
episodes.212886: Warm temperatures and moist upslope winds fueled thunderstorm development in eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the 15th. This cluster of thunderstorms moved into West Texas during the evening hours producing isolated wind damage. It was reported that power poles were snapped in Parmer County while shingles were blown off of a roof in Abernathy.
episodes.212945: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.
episodes.213081: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Indiana during the afternoon of June 16th producing isolated large hail.
episodes.213519: On the afternoon on June 16, a few supercells developed. Photos of wall clouds were received and hail as large as 2 inches in diameter was recorded (in Michigan). Two EF-U tornadoes occurred as well.
episodes.213520: On the afternoon on June 16, a few supercells developed. Photos of wall clouds were received and hail as large as 2 inches in diameter was recorded.
episodes.213603: An upper-level low which had been nearly stationary over Hudson Bay in Canada was producing several disturbances moving across the upper Midwest in early to mid-June.  On June 15th, enough mid-level instability and surface moisture was in place to generate scattered showers and thunderstorms that afternoon. In Mille Lacs County, one storm briefly pulsed up strong enough to produce a 67-mph wind gust approximately 9 miles north of Milaca. The storm continued southeast into Isanti County where a couple trees were downed in Dalbo and Stanchfield.
episodes.213762: Isolated thunderstorms developed in a moist, warm environment with just enough instability and wind shear to allow them to become severe. Hail was the main hazard with these storms.
episodes.214102: Multiple rounds of flash flooding occurred throughout Southeast Texas over the course of several days, leading up to Tropical storm Arthur.
episodes.214145: A seabreeze which was pinned along the Crystal Coast combined with a stalled frontal boundary to produce a cluster of thunderstorms near the New River and White Oak River during the afternoon of June sixteenth. With enhanced helicity values due to the stalled front being around the area, a few of these storms became strong in nature with a thunderstorm producing a waterspout along the White Oak River.
episodes.214199: A few thunderstorms produced 1-inch hail in Oakland County.
episodes.214204: A thunderstorms moving trough Saginaw Bay produced a wind gust in excessive of 35 knots.
episodes.214348: Despite nebulous synoptic forcing and modest instability, several supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a weak surface cold front across southwestern Kansas into far northwestern Oklahoma during the evening hours of the 16th. One such thunderstorm produced large to very large hail in Harper County, Oklahoma before dissipating.
episodes.214467: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.214481: Middle June saw a disturbance track over the Central Brooks Range resulting in anywhere from 1 to 1.5 inches of rain in about a 24 hour period. While most rivers were ice free, plenty of snowpack remained across the higher slopes. With high temperatures generally in the 60's and overnight lows remaining above freezing, excessive snowmelt combined with heavy rainfall lead to rapid rises along area streams and rivers, including the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River. As a result, flooding was reported from Coldfoot to Wiseman.
episodes.214514: A weather pattern in the upper atmosphere favored the development of showers and thunderstorms across the local area. At the surface, a stalled frontal boundary stretched from west to east near the I-10 corridor and provided a focus for repeated thunderstorm development. Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of coastal Mississippi over the two-day period and resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.214515: A weather pattern in the upper atmosphere favored the development of showers and thunderstorms across the area. At the surface, a stalled frontal boundary stretched from west to east near the I-12 corridor and provided a focus for repeated thunderstorm development. Thunderstorms repeatedly developed and moved over the same areas along the boundary, producing very heavy rainfall across portions of metro Baton Rouge and the Northshore region of metro New Orleans and resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.214545: A broken line of thunderstorms developed over east central IL during the afternoon of June 16th.  These low topped supercells produced several large hail reports over Champaign and Vermilion Counties.  The largest hailstone recorded was the size of a golf ball.
episodes.214659: A mid-level disturbance rotated through cyclonic northwest flow established over the Northern Plains. Scattered storms developed along a weak surface convergence boundary with minimal MLCAPE around 500 J/kg during the afternoon, but managed to yield an isolated damaging wind gust in southeast South Dakota and isolated large hail in southwest Minnesota.
episodes.214660: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 15-19 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported, and one tornado was confirmed in Washington county.
episodes.215061: Fueled by the heating of the day, scattered thunderstorms developed across primarily central and east-central Wisconsin during the late morning and afternoon hours on June 16, 2026. Cold temperatures aloft resulted in low freezing levels and efficient hail production in storms. Most hail was just below severe criteria, though a storm over Fond du Lac and Sheboygan County grew strong enough to produce localized severe hail.
episodes.215663: Training storms along a slowly sagging boundary produced heavy rainfall focused in the far southern portion of the CWA. A flash flood warning was issued for portions of Marion, Lamar, and Forrest Counties and flash flooding occurred in Forrest County.
episodes.215670: A weak frontal boundary drifted into southeast Texas well ahead of Tropical Storm Arthur. Heavy rain produced areas of flooding.
episodes.215703: Tropical Storm Arthur made landfall along the coast of southeast Texas and moved northeast across central Louisiana. Heavy rain trained across portions of central Louisiana creating widespread flooding and a new rainfall record. Flood waters slowly drained in the days following the passage of the system.
episodes.215846: Thunderstorms with large hail impacted parts of lower Michigan on June 16-17.
episodes.215874: Broad cyclonic flow and subtle shortwave energy aloft along with a weak surface boundary and ample moisture in the vicinity led to an environment capable for a strong thunderstorm across local waters.

events.narrative: Up to 1.5 inches of warm rain fell on remaining snowpack across the Central Brooks range resulting in a rapid rise of the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River between Coldfoot and Wiseman. Late evening on Monday the 15th, the public reported that water was moving over the road to Wiseman. A social media comment on the NWS Warning post came in just after midnight on the 16th stating that the water was high enough that it would be very difficult if not impossible to get in or out of Wiseman by road. In addition the NWS received reports from the general public stating that the water came up very fast, but did begin to slowly subside through the day on the 16th as the rain tapered off and came to an end.
